title: Silbo Gomero
hook: On one Canary Island, people can hold a conversation by whistling Spanish.
peek: On La Gomera, a steep island in the Canaries, Spanish can be whistled. Silbo Gomero turns words into rising and falling whistles that carry across deep ravines, and every child on the island learns it at school.
lede: La Gomera is a small, steep island in the Canaries, cut by deep ravines. Walking to a neighbour could take an hour, but a whistle crosses the valley in seconds. So islanders developed Silbo Gomero, a way of whistling Spanish. It is not a code of signals: skilled whistlers can say almost anything they could say aloud.

bullets.opening: Older than Spanish on the island
bullets.text: Historians think the island's first inhabitants already whistled their own language before the Spanish arrived in the fifteenth century. Over time, the whistling was carried over to Spanish.

Whistlers put a finger or two in the mouth and cup the other hand to aim the sound. Silbo replaces speech sounds with changes in pitch and breaks in the whistle; linguists usually describe two vowel sounds and a handful of consonants, and listeners fill in words from context.
A strong whistle can be understood far beyond the reach of a shout, often said to be a few kilometres in good conditions. Shepherds and farmers used it to pass messages across the island.
As roads and phones arrived, Silbo nearly faded. Since 1999 it has been taught in La Gomera's schools, and in 2009 UNESCO added it to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
